title: Orbit versus Orbital — and the Spherical s Orbital
topicTitle: Orbitals and shape of s and p orbitals only
notes: The orbit–orbital distinction in tabular form plus the s-orbital details (radial probability distribution) that the main note covers briefly.
• Nature: fixed 2D circular path / 3D probability region.
• Definiteness: exact radius and momentum / neither is definite (Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π).
• Number: one orbit per n / n² orbitals per shell.
• Direction: non-directional concept / s spherical, p directional.
• Status: contradicted by experiment / the accepted modern picture.
• Shape: sphere — electron density depends only on distance r, not direction (non-directional, hence s orbitals give no directionality in bonding).

• Radial probability distribution: the chance of finding the electron between r and r + dr peaks at the most probable distance — 0.529 Å for 1s. For 2s the curve has two maxima separated by a radial node where probability is exactly zero.
• Nodes: 1s none; 2s one spherical node at r = 2a₀ ≈ 1.06 Å; 3s two; in general (n − 1) spherical nodes. There are no nodal planes for s.
• Size and energy: both increase with n (1s < 2s < 3s), and higher s orbitals penetrate closer to the nucleus than p of the same shell — the origin of the ns < np energy order.

Spherical symmetry makes s orbitals the 'all-direction' bond formers (H uses 1s in every bond), the mixing component of every hybrid (sp, sp², sp³), and the reason the noble-gas electron clouds (filled s and p) are spherically symmetric — the chemical basis of their inertness.
confusion: ❌ 2s is just a bigger 1s. ✅ 2s also has an inner radial node and a second probability maximum — qualitatively different.
❌ The electron sits on the surface of the drawn sphere. ✅ The sphere is a probability boundary; the density decays continuously outward.
❌ s orbitals can be directional after hybridisation. ✅ Pure s is spherical; directionality appears only in hybrid orbitals (sp, sp², sp³).

universalFacts: The 1s radial probability maximum lies at exactly a₀ = 0.529 Å.
The 2s radial node lies at r = 2a₀ ≈ 1.06 Å — probability is zero there.
s orbitals are the only subshells present in every shell (n = 1 to ∞).
examples: **Problem:** Compare the probability of finding the 1s electron at r = a₀ and r = 0. **Solution:** the *radial probability* 4πr²|ψ|² vanishes at r = 0 (the r² factor) and peaks at a₀ — even though |ψ|² itself is largest at the nucleus; the two curves answer different questions.
importantNotes: Distinguish |ψ|² (probability density, maximal at the nucleus for 1s) from radial probability (maximal at a₀) — a classic subtlety.

summary: Orbit and orbital differ in origin, nature, definiteness, number, direction and status: an orbit is Bohr's fixed two-dimensional circular path with an exact radius and momentum, while an orbital is Schrödinger's three-dimensional probability region with neither quantity definite (Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π); there is one orbit per n but n² orbitals per shell, and only orbitals have direction. The s orbital in detail is spherical, so its density depends only on r and it is non-directional; its radial probability distribution P(r) = 4πr²|ψ|² peaks at the most probable distance, 0.529 Å for 1s, and for 2s it shows two maxima separated by a spherical radial node at r = 2a₀ ≈ 1.06 Å, with (n − 1) such nodes in general and no nodal plane at all. Size and energy rise with n, and s orbitals penetrate closer to the nucleus than p of the same shell, which is the origin of the ns < np order.
importantConcepts: Six-row contrast: origin (Bohr versus Schrödinger), nature (2D path versus 3D region), definiteness, number, direction and status
s orbital: spherical, non-directional, present in every shell, with P(r) = 4πr²|ψ|² peaking at 0.529 Å for 1s
Radial nodes: (n − 1) spherical nodes and no nodal plane; the 2s node lies at r = 2a₀ ≈ 1.06 Å
Size and energy both increase with n, and s orbitals penetrate closer to the nucleus than p, giving ns < np
Chemical role: s orbitals are the all-direction bond formers and the mixing component of every sp, sp² and sp³ hybrid
importantStatements: An orbital is a region of maximum probability with no sharp edge; the electron may be found outside the drawn sphere.
|ψ|² is largest at the nucleus for 1s, but the radial probability 4πr²|ψ|² peaks at a₀ = 0.529 Å.
2s is not merely a bigger 1s: it has an inner radial node and a second probability maximum.
s orbitals are the only subshells present in every shell, from n = 1 upwards.
Pure s orbitals cannot be directional; directionality appears only after hybridisation.

keyPoints: One orbit per n; n² orbitals per shell.
Radial nodes = n − 1 for s orbitals; angular nodes = 0.
1s radial probability maximum = a₀ = 0.529 Å; 2s node = 2a₀ ≈ 1.06 Å.
Spherical symmetry explains the inertness of noble gases, whose filled s and p shells give a spherically symmetric cloud.
specialNotes: Probability density and radial probability answer different questions and peak at different places — a classic subtlety.
Higher s orbitals are larger and more penetrating but never directional or dumbbell-shaped.
The drawn sphere is a boundary surface at a chosen probability, not a container.
examShortTricks: Use the six-row table format for the orbit-versus-orbital question; it matches the marking scheme.
Radial probability P(r) = 4πr²|ψ|² — the r² factor is why it vanishes at r = 0 while |ψ|² does not.
Quote 0.529 Å as the most probable distance, never as a fixed radius.

Applications to bonding and hybridisation usually close the question.
